paragraphs: “We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, with his head battered in,” said the prosecutor.
“That’s horrible!” Mitya shuddered and, putting his elbows on the table, hid his face in his right hand.
“We will continue,” Nikolay Parfenovitch broke in. “So what was it that drove you to this hatred? I believe you have said in public that it was based on jealousy?”
“Well, yes, jealousy. And not only jealousy.”
“Quarrels about money?”
“Yes, about money, too.”
“There was a dispute about three thousand roubles, I think, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?”

“Three thousand! More, more,” cried Mitya hotly. “More than six thousand, more than ten, maybe. I told everyone so, shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to let it go at three thousand. I badly needed that three thousand ... so the bundle of notes for three thousand that I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I considered simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I looked on it as mine, as my own property....”
The prosecutor looked meaningfully at the investigating lawyer, and found time to wink at him on the sly.
“We will come back to that subject later,” the lawyer said promptly. “You will allow us to note that point and write it down: that you looked on that money as your own property?”

“Write it down, by all means. I know that’s another fact that tells against me, but I’m not afraid of facts, and I tell them against myself. Do you hear? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different sort of man from what I am,” he added, suddenly gloomy and dejected. “You’re dealing with a man of honor, a man of the highest honor. Above all—don’t lose sight of it—a man who’s done a lot of nasty things, but has always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, in his inner being. I don’t know how to put it. That’s just what’s made me wretched all my life, that I yearned to be honorable, that I was, so to say, a martyr to a sense of honor, looking for it with a lantern, with the lantern of Diogenes, and yet all my life I’ve been doing filthy things like all of us, gentlemen ... that is, like me alone. That was a mistake, like me alone, me alone!... Gentlemen, my head aches ...” His brows contracted with pain. “You see, gentlemen, I couldn’t bear the sight of him. There was something in him ignoble, impudent, trampling on everything sacred, something sneering and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he’s dead, I feel differently.”
“How do you mean?”
“I don’t feel differently, but I wish I hadn’t hated him so.”
“You feel remorse?”
“No, not remorse, don’t write that. I’m not much good myself, I’m not very beautiful, so I had no right to think him repulsive. That’s what I mean. Write that down, if you like.”
As he said this, Mitya became very mournful. He had grown more and more gloomy as the inquiry went on.

At that moment another unexpected scene followed. Grushenka had been taken away, but not far. She was only in the room next but one to the blue room where the examination was going on. It was a little room with one window, just beyond the large room where they had danced and feasted so lavishly. She was sitting there with no one beside her but Maximov, who was terribly depressed and terribly scared and clung to her side as though for safety. At their door stood one of the peasants with a metal plate on his chest. Grushenka was crying. Suddenly her grief was too much for her. She jumped up, threw up her arms and, with a loud wail of sorrow, rushed out of the room to him, to her Mitya. It happened so unexpectedly that they had no time to stop her. Mitya heard her cry and trembled. He jumped up and, with a yell, rushed to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they were not allowed to come together, though they saw one another. He was seized by the arms. He struggled and tried to tear himself away. It took three or four men to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her stretching out her arms to him and crying aloud as they carried her away. When the scene was over, he came to himself again, sitting in the same place as before, opposite the investigating lawyer, and crying out to them:
“What do you want with her? Why do you torment her? She’s done nothing, nothing!...”
The lawyers tried to soothe him. About ten minutes went by like this. At last Mihail Makarovitch, who had been away, came hurrying into the room and said to the prosecutor in a loud, excited voice:
“She’s been taken away, she’s downstairs. Will you allow me to say one word to this unhappy man, gentlemen? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence.”
“By all means, Mihail Makarovitch,” answered the investigating lawyer. “In this case we have no objection.”

“Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow,” the police captain began, and his excited face showed warm, almost fatherly feeling for the luckless prisoner. “I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself and left her in the care of the landlord’s daughters, and that old fellow Maximov is with her all the time. And I soothed her, do you hear? I soothed and calmed her. I made it clear to her that you have to clear yourself, so she mustn’t get in your way, mustn’t depress you, or you might lose your head and say the wrong thing in your evidence. In short, I talked to her and she understood. She’s a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl. She would have kissed my old hands, asking help for you. She sent me herself to tell you not to worry about her. And I must go, my dear fellow, I must go and tell her that you are calm and comforted about her. So you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her. She is a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, she’s a gentle soul, and not to blame for anything. So what am I to tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quiet or not?”

The good-natured police captain said a great deal that was irregular. But Grushenka’s suffering, the suffering of a fellow creature, touched his kind heart, and tears stood in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

“Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!” he cried. “You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch, I thank you for her. I will, I will be calm, cheerful, in fact. Tell her, in the kindness of your heart, that I am cheerful, quite cheerful, that I’ll be laughing in a minute, knowing that she has a guardian angel like you. I’ll be done with all this at once, and as soon as I’m free, I’ll be with her, she’ll see, let her wait. Gentlemen,” he said, turning to the two lawyers, “now I’ll open my whole soul to you. I’ll pour out everything. We’ll finish this off at once, finish it off gaily. We’ll laugh at it in the end, won’t we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That one thing I’ll tell you now.... I see I’m among honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, ‘I’ll go to death with you’? And what have I, a penniless beggar, done for her? Why does she love me so? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with my ugly face, deserve such love, that she’s ready to go into exile with me? And how she fell down at your feet for my sake, just now!... and yet she’s proud and has done nothing! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her as I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I am comforted.”

And he sank back in his chair and, covering his face with his hands, burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He recovered himself instantly. The old police captain seemed very pleased, and so did the lawyers. They felt that the examination was moving into a new phase. When the police captain went out, Mitya was positively gay.

“Now, gentlemen, I am at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren’t for all these trivial details, we’d understand one another in a minute. There I go with the details again. I’m at your disposal, gentlemen, but I declare that we must have mutual confidence, you in me and I in you, or there’ll be no end to it. I’m speaking in your interests. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don’t rummage in my soul. Don’t tease me with trifles, but ask me only about facts and what matters, and I’ll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!”
So spoke Mitya. The interrogation began again.
